title: Before optimising, check the objective against an energy identity and its gradient against finite differences, and plot the error, not just the two values
summary: A bar chart compares two ways of computing the power dissipated in a channel flow, and a pair of panels compares an analytic design gradient with central finite differences at two step sizes. Both are pre-optimisation gates: their purpose is to show a small number, so the figure must make small numbers visible.

media.alt: Two panels against design strip index 1 to 6. Left: the analytic gradient as a blue line with markers between 1.383e-15 and 1.440e-15, with red crosses and plus signs for two central finite-difference step sizes lying exactly on it; the y axis spans only 1.38e-15 to 1.44e-15. Right: relative error between finite-difference and analytic gradient on a log axis, between about 1e-11 and 2e-10 for both step sizes, far below a dotted reference line at 1e-6.

source.caption: Analytic design-sensitivity gradient compared with finite differences
group: 08_mfv_d4_gradient_vs_finite_differences: Analytic design-sensitivity gradient compared with finite differences (representative)
source.note: The page teaches the generic reading of an energy-identity check and of a gradient-versus-finite-difference check with standard theory only; numbers quoted are printed on the figures, read from them, or computed in the Apply script. The cfdcore project holds near-identical figures with their own explainer.

read_the_figure.question: Is the quantity that will be minimised computed consistently, and is its analytic derivative with respect to each design variable correct?
read_the_figure.axes: Power identity: two groups of bars, one per form of the viscous term; blue is the dissipation integral, grey is pressure drop times flow rate, y in watts per metre (two-dimensional, per unit depth) with a 1e-7 multiplier; the printed E is the relative difference. Gradient: x is the design strip index 1 to 6; left y is the derivative of the dissipation with respect to that strip's friction value (units m^4/s^2), right y is the relative error of the finite-difference derivative on a log axis from 1e-11 to 1e-6.
look_at: Bars: in each pair the blue and grey bars look equal; the printed E is 0.08 percent and 0.18 percent, which no bar height could show.
Bars: the two viscous forms give nearly the same height, about 1.37e-7.
Gradient, left: the analytic line passes through every finite-difference marker; the y axis is zoomed to a 4 percent band, so the strip-to-strip wiggle is magnified.
Gradient, right: both step sizes give 1e-11 to 2e-10, four to five orders below the dotted reference at 1e-6.
Gradient, right: the error is not 100 times smaller for the smaller step.
read_the_figure.proves: The identity check shows that the dissipation integral and the externally supplied power agree to about a tenth of a percent on this mesh for two forms of the viscous term. The gradient check shows the analytic derivative agrees with a finite-difference estimate to about 1e-10 for all six strips and both steps, passing a 1e-6 gate by a large margin.
if_wrong: Bars that differ by a visible amount: a missing term in the objective, a different boundary condition for the integral and the power, or a mesh too coarse.
Gradient errors near 1: a sign or factor error in the analytic derivative.
Errors that fall as h^2 until a floor then rise as 1/h: normal finite-difference behaviour; a floor higher than the gate means noise from the solver tolerance.
Agreement for one strip but not another: a bug that depends on position, such as a missing boundary term.
must_check: The identity's assumptions (boundary conditions, which traction terms vanish) are stated.
A mesh refinement shows the error falls, otherwise 'discretisation-error level' is asserted, not shown.
The error, not the two values, is plotted on a log axis when the agreement is high.
Both a larger and a smaller finite-difference step are shown so truncation and rounding can be told apart.
The y axis of a value plot is not zoomed so that agreement looks like structure.
as_drawn: Bars: first pair about 1.37e-7 W/m each, E = 0.08 percent; second pair about 1.365e-7 each, E = 0.18 percent; one mesh only. Label: PASS, agreement at FEM discretization-error level.
Gradient values by strip (read, units 1e-15 m^4/s^2): about 1.383, 1.430, 1.405, 1.440, 1.413, 1.432. Left y axis spans 1.38 to 1.44.

Relative errors: step 1e-3 gives about 1.4e-10, 1.3e-10, 1e-11, 3.5e-11, 3.2e-11, 5e-11; step 1e-2 gives about 1.0e-10, 1.6e-10, 1.35e-10, 1.35e-10, 1.4e-10, 1.9e-10. Label: PASS, agreement to about 1e-10 for both step sizes.

terms.meaning: The rate at which flow work is turned into heat by viscosity, plus here a friction term; for the flows in this project it equals the work done by the pressure drop.
An exact relation between two quantities that must hold for the true solution, such as dissipation equals pressure drop times flow rate.
The derivative of the objective with respect to a design variable, here the friction value in one strip of the design region.
A derivative estimate from two evaluations on either side of the point; its truncation error shrinks as h squared.
An objective for which the adjoint problem equals the original flow problem, so the gradient needs only the flow solution and no extra solve.
The absolute difference divided by the size of the reference, so a value of 1e-10 means about ten correct digits.
A threshold that a check must pass before the next stage of work proceeds.

remember: An energy identity is a free exact test: no reference solution is needed.
A pre-optimisation gradient check compares analytic and finite-difference derivatives on every design variable.
When agreement is good, plot the error on a log axis; bars or overlaid lines cannot show it.
Central differences have a truncation error falling as h squared and a rounding error growing as one over h.
A zoomed y axis turns small differences between neighbours into visible structure.

understand.title: Why dissipation equals pressure drop times flow rate
understand.text: Multiply the momentum equation by the velocity and integrate. The viscous and friction terms give the dissipation integral. The pressure and traction terms reduce to boundary integrals, and with a pressure difference between inlet and outlet and negligible viscous traction there, they equal the pressure drop times the volume flow rate. Nothing about the geometry matters, so this is a test of the whole discrete system.

understand.title: Two forms of the viscous term
understand.text: For incompressible flow the integrand 2 mu D:D and the simpler mu |grad u|^2 differ by a divergence term, which integrates to a boundary contribution. Their closeness here, 0.08 and 0.18 percent from the external power, shows the boundary contribution is small for this configuration, and the small difference between them is a measure of how well the outlet conditions approximate fully developed flow.

understand.title: Why the gradient needs no extra solve
understand.text: For an objective that is the energy of the flow at fixed flux, the first-order change due to a change of the friction in one cell comes only from the explicit friction term, because the flow adjusts to minimise the energy. So the derivative with respect to strip e is the integral of the squared velocity over that strip, as the legend states.

understand.title: What the finite-difference errors say
understand.text: Truncation error would fall by 100 times when the step falls by 10; rounding error would grow by 10 times. Here both steps give errors of the same order, 1e-11 to 2e-10, so neither pattern dominates and the number is probably set by something else, such as the tolerance of the linear solve. The conclusion that the gradient is right does not depend on that, since the floor is far below the gate.

steps.title: Dissipation functional
steps.tex: \Phi(\mathbf u)=\int_\Omega\left(2\mu\,\mathbf D(\mathbf u):\mathbf D(\mathbf u)+\alpha|\mathbf u|^{2}\right)d\Omega
steps.note: D is the symmetric part of the velocity gradient; alpha is the Brinkman friction, varying by design strip.

steps.title: Energy identity
steps.note: Pressure drop times volume flow rate per unit depth, in watts per metre, the units of the bar chart.

steps.title: Relative gap between the bars
steps.note: The printed E values are 0.08 and 0.18 percent.

steps.title: Gradient of a self-adjoint objective
steps.note: For dissipation at fixed flux. This is the analytic expression named in the legend; units are m^2/s^2 times m^2 per unit depth, that is m^4/s^2.

steps.title: Central finite difference
steps.note: Evaluate the objective twice per design variable with a fresh flow solve each time. The step h is a fraction of alpha_e: the legend's 1e-3 and 1e-2.

steps.title: Rounding floor
steps.note: The truncation term falls with h and the noise term rises, so the best step balances them. The two panels show errors far below 1e-6, so the noise floor is not a concern here.

worked.title: How big is the gap between the bars?
worked.problem: Each bar is about 1.37e-7 W/m and the printed E for the first pair is 0.08 percent. The bar axis spans 0 to 1.85e-7 and the plot area is about 540 pixels tall. How many pixels is the gap, and what does that say about the chart?

solution.text: The fraction of the axis height.

worked.answer: About a third of a pixel: the bars cannot show the agreement, so the printed E values carry the whole claim. A log-scale plot of E against mesh size would show it and its trend. The pixel height is an approximate read from the displayed figure.

analyze.q: In the toy script the finite-difference error falls 100 times when the step falls 10 times. In the figure it does not. List two possible reasons and one test to tell them apart.
analyze.hint: Floor from the linear solver, or nearly linear response.

analyze.q: The left panel's y axis spans 1.38e-15 to 1.44e-15. How large is the strip-to-strip variation as a percentage of the mean, and what would a zero-based axis show?
The two viscous forms give E of 0.08 and 0.18 percent. If one is exactly equal to the identity for the true solution, what would you expect the other to do under mesh refinement?
analyze.hint: The boundary term they differ by is a discretisation quantity.

evaluate.q: The bar-chart banner says agreement is 'at discretization-error level'. What evidence would make that statement a result and not an assumption?
A gradient check passes at 1e-10 for six strips. Does that clear a gradient for hundreds of design variables?
evaluate.hint: Which strips, which designs, which flow states were tested.

create: Redraw the identity check as relative error E against mesh size on log-log axes for both viscous forms, with a slope reference, so that agreement and convergence are visible.
Design a gradient check for many design variables that avoids one flow solve per variable per step: say which subset you test, how you choose it, and what you report.

checks.q: Why does dissipation equal pressure drop times flow rate?
checks.hint: Multiply the momentum equation by u and integrate.
checks.answer: The volume integral of the viscous and friction terms equals the boundary work, which for a pressure-driven channel with negligible viscous traction is the pressure drop times the flow rate.

checks.q: A bar is 1.37e-7 W/m and E is 0.18 percent. What is the absolute gap?
Why should a good gradient check show errors for two different step sizes?
checks.hint: What do truncation and rounding errors do as h changes?
checks.answer: Truncation error falls with h and rounding error rises, so two steps show whether the error is dominated by either and whether the agreement is robust.

checks.q: The identity check has one mesh. What is the limitation?
checks.hint: What does a convergence claim need?
checks.answer: The error is a single number; without refinement one cannot say whether it is discretisation error or a modelling difference, nor whether it decreases.

checks.q: How would you make a gradient gate part of a routine run?
checks.hint: Think of a check that can fail automatically.
checks.answer: Compute analytic and central-difference derivatives for a random subset of design variables at every release, fail if the relative error exceeds the gate, and log it by variable.

provenance.notes: Disclosure: the images carry PASS banners, internal parameter names (viscous_form=laplacian and stress on the bar chart, a g_fd, g_analytic and h_rel notation, an 'alpha_e' strip label), a D.3/D.4 milestone prefix and a phrase naming the objective 'topology optimization minimizes' and 'the pre-optimization gate'. None are repeated; the page teaches the generic reading. Owner review: (1) the bar chart cannot display a 0.1 percent difference; the printed E values are the evidence. (2) 'discretization-error level' is asserted from a single mesh. (3) The left gradient panel zooms the y axis to a 4 percent band, exaggerating strip-to-strip variation. (4) The finite-difference errors do not scale as h^2 between the two steps, so the 1e-10 floor is probably solver-tolerance limited; the figure does not say. (5) The analytic formula is stated in the legend as the integral of |u|^2 over the strip; check it is meant as the fixed-flux dissipation derivative, as the page assumes.
